items.prompt: What is an architectural style?
choices: A recurring shape that answers recurring pressures
A framework you install before the first commit
A ranking of which technology is the most modern
items.explanation: A style is a reusable shape tied to the pressures it handles.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows a style was chosen as a decision?
choices: Everyone says that this shape is the modern way to build
Our pricing rules change weekly, and this shape isolates them
Our competitor uses it, so we should adopt it too
items.explanation: A decision names what will change and how the style protects against it.

items.prompt: A style is best described as a bet about what?
choices: Which kind of change is going to hurt the most
Which programming language will be fastest to run
Which engineers on the team will stay longest
items.explanation: The bet is about the axis of change, made before the pain appears.

items.prompt: Someone says 'we should use microservices' and cannot say why. What is that?
choices: A decision, because microservices are popular
A decision, because it is a recognized style
A buzzword, not a decision
items.explanation: Without a named pressure, the style was picked for its name.

items.prompt: Do the four styles rank from worst to best?
choices: Yes, layered is the worst and microservices the best
Yes, newer styles are always better than older ones
No, each protects against a different kind of pain
items.explanation: They are different bets, not a ladder.

items.prompt: When should the style be chosen, relative to the pain?
choices: Before the pain shows up
Only after the pain has become severe
Never; it should emerge by accident
items.explanation: A style is a bet made ahead of time about where the pain will land.

items.prompt: What does 'X' stand for in 'we choose this because our X will change'?
choices: The cost of the cloud bill at the end of the month
The named thing under pressure, such as rules or integrations
The number of engineers who dislike the old design
items.explanation: X is the specific axis of change the style protects.

items.prompt: Which question starts a sound style choice?
choices: Which style has the nicest diagrams?
Which style did the last project use?
What is most likely to change here?
items.explanation: Starting from what varies keeps the choice tied to real forces.

items.prompt: A team writes in its design doc: 'We will adopt event-driven because it is the industry direction.' What is the flaw?
choices: Event-driven designs can never be used in one app
No pressure is named that the shape would absorb
Industry direction is always a wrong reason to adopt
The doc should have named at least three styles first
items.explanation: The sentence never says what will change; without that, the choice is a badge.
items.reference:
A style is a bet, not a badge
decision: names the X that will change or grow
buzzword: picked because the name sounds modern
test: finish 'we choose this because our X will change...'
no X named: no decision has been made yet
Why: a style is chosen to protect against a named kind of change, not for its fashionable name.
items.learnMore:
Style as a decision

A style records which kind of pain you expect (rules changing, integrations changing, teams colliding) and picks a shape that absorbs it. If you cannot name the pain, the choice has no reason behind it.

Common mistake

Treating a style name as a quality mark. Microservices are not better than a layered app; they answer different pressures.
items.reflection: Think of a tool or process choice outside software that someone defended with its name rather than a named problem. What would the missing 'because our X will change' have been?

items.prompt: Which statement completes the test sentence well?
choices: Our team enjoys learning new architectural vocabulary and wants practice using it
Larger systems are generally expected to use more services
Integrations with partners change monthly and must not block checkout
We would like the diagram to look balanced to reviewers
items.explanation: Only the first names a concrete changing thing and a protection the style offers.

items.prompt: Which style puts the business rules in the center with outside tools plugged in?
choices: Layered
Event-driven
Hexagonal / clean
items.explanation: The center knows nothing external; tools attach through ports.

items.prompt: Which style splits the running system into independently deployed services?
choices: Microservices
Layered
Hexagonal / clean
items.explanation: Independent deployment of separate services is the defining trait.

items.prompt: What is layered architecture's main weakness?
choices: It cannot run on a single server
Rules can quietly leak into the wrong layer
It forces every part to be deployed alone
items.explanation: Nothing structurally stops a layer from reaching where it should not.

items.prompt: What does event-driven buy?
choices: Instantly correct data in every component
The easiest bugs to trace in the system
A slow receiver does not block the sender
items.explanation: The sender publishes and returns, so receiver delays stay with the receiver.

items.prompt: What is the main cost of event-driven?
choices: Data may only be correct a little later
More engineers are needed in each team
Every call must go through a database table
items.explanation: Eventual consistency and scattered traces are the price.

items.prompt: What does hexagonal cost you compared with layered?
choices: The ability to write any automated tests
More files and more indirection
The option of storing data in a database
items.explanation: Ports and adapters add structure the plain version avoids.

items.prompt: Which style is cheapest to start and easiest to explain?
choices: Layered
Microservices
Event-driven
items.explanation: A few layers in one app need the least setup.

items.prompt: What does a microservices split add that a single app does not have?
choices: A guarantee that the code is well designed
Automatic removal of coupling between features
Network calls where function calls used to be
items.explanation: Calls between parts now cross a network and can fail partway.

items.prompt: A small team wants the business rules testable without a database or web framework. Which style's main benefit is that?
choices: Layered, because each layer only calls the one below it
Hexagonal, because the domain sits behind ports it owns
Event-driven, because handlers can be unit tested alone
Microservices, because each service has its own database
items.explanation: Only hexagonal makes the domain independent of infrastructure by construction.
items.reference:
What each style buys and costs
layered: cheap start / rules can leak between layers
hexagonal: testable core / more files and indirection
event-driven: sender not blocked / data correct later
microservices: independent releases / network and ops weight
Why: each style pays for one benefit with one specific cost.
items.learnMore:
The trade each style makes

Every style gives up something to protect something else. Layered protects simplicity, hexagonal protects the domain from infrastructure, event-driven protects the sender from a slow receiver, microservices protect teams from waiting on each other.

Common mistake

Remembering only the benefits. Each benefit comes with a cost that is easy to forget until it arrives.
items.reflection: Pick a trade you made in daily life, like a cheaper option that cost you flexibility. Which of the four styles' trade-offs does it most resemble?

items.prompt: Which pairing of style and its characteristic cost is correct?
choices: Layered with a separate deployment pipeline per layer
Hexagonal with delays caused by a shared message bus
Event-driven with data that is correct a little later
Microservices with rules that leak between layers in one app
items.explanation: Eventual consistency belongs to event-driven; the other pairings mix up costs.

items.prompt: Which question separates layered or hexagonal from event-driven?
choices: How many files does each style generate?
Which style has the shortest name to type?
What changes most: the rules or the systems we talk to?
items.explanation: Rules favor layered or hexagonal; integrations favor event-driven.

items.prompt: One engineer will own the whole system. What does that say about microservices?
choices: There is little to gain from them
They are required for any single owner
They are the safest default choice
items.explanation: Microservices decouple teams; one owner has nobody to decouple from.

items.prompt: Which coupling is more expensive to fix?
choices: A tangled layered app, which needs a repository-wide rewrite
Tangled services, which need coordinated multi-team deploys
Both cost exactly the same amount to untangle
items.explanation: A bad service boundary is a migration; a bad layer is a refactor.

items.prompt: Loyalty points must be exactly right when the order is placed. What does that argue against?
choices: A design where the points arrive later
A design that keeps everything in one app
A design that has well-tested business rules
items.explanation: Eventual consistency cannot meet an instant-correctness requirement.

items.prompt: How many questions does this unit suggest asking before picking a style?
choices: Two
Nine
Four
items.explanation: Rules vs integrations, people and teams, cost of coupling, tolerance for delay.

items.prompt: Which question is about time?
choices: How many engineers are on the team today?
Which framework does the front end use?
Can we accept data that is correct a little later?
items.explanation: Question four asks about tolerating delayed correctness.

items.prompt: Three separate teams share one codebase and block each other's deploys. Which question surfaces that?
choices: How many people and how many teams?
Can data be correct a little later?
What changes most often here?
items.explanation: Team count shows where independent deployment would help.

items.prompt: What should happen before any code is written?
choices: The first style is installed from a template
The four questions are answered
The service count is fixed in advance
items.explanation: The questions are asked before code, when changes are cheapest.

items.prompt: A solo developer's app has rules that change daily and no partner integrations. Which choice best matches the questions?
choices: Microservices, so each rule gets its own service
Event-driven, because every rule change is an event
Hexagonal with each adapter deployed as a separate service
Plain layered, or hexagonal if testability matters
items.explanation: One owner and fast-changing rules point to a single deployable app, not a split.
items.reference:
Four questions before code
1. what changes: rules or integrations?
2. how many people and teams?
3. what does wrong coupling cost to fix?
4. can data be correct a little later?
Why: the answers point at a style; the styles do not point at themselves.
items.learnMore:
Questions before names

Asking the four questions first turns an argument about taste into a short fact-finding exercise. The answers rarely all point the same way, which is why the choice is a judgment and not a lookup.

Common mistake

Answering question 4 last or not at all. Eventual consistency is the cost that most often comes as a surprise.
items.reflection: Think about a decision you recently made quickly. Which of the four questions (what changes, how many people, cost of being wrong, tolerance for delay) would have changed your answer if you had asked it first?

items.prompt: Which requirement should make you doubt an event-driven design?
choices: Several teams want to react to the same order
Points must be correct the instant the order completes
The receiving partner is slow and sometimes down
Analytics should be updated without delaying checkout for any customer
items.explanation: Instant correctness conflicts with eventual consistency; the others are what events suit.

items.prompt: What does an import mean in this unit?
choices: One file depends on another file's code
A file gets copied over onto another server
A function is deleted from a file
items.explanation: Importing creates a dependency on the other file.

items.prompt: In hexagonal architecture, who imports whom?
choices: The domain imports the adapters it needs
Adapters import the domain's ports
Neither ever imports the other
items.explanation: The arrow always points inward toward the domain.

items.prompt: Can the domain import a database client in a hexagonal codebase?
choices: Yes, if it is wrapped in a folder
Yes, whenever it is convenient
No
items.explanation: That would reverse the dependency direction.

items.prompt: Which style's folder tree can look almost identical to hexagonal's?
choices: Layered
Microservices
Event-driven
items.explanation: Both live in one app, so the difference is in the imports.

items.prompt: Where does the real difference between layered and hexagonal show up?
choices: In how many separate servers each one uses
In which direction imports may point
In the color of the diagram boxes
items.explanation: Direction is the structural rule; folder listings hide it.

items.prompt: What is a port?
choices: An interface the domain defines for outside tools to meet
A network cable connecting two services
A database table that stores domain rules
items.explanation: Ports are owned by the domain; adapters implement them.

items.prompt: What is an adapter in hexagonal architecture?
choices: A test that checks business rules
A layer that holds all the domain rules
Code that connects an outside tool to a port
items.explanation: Adapters translate between the outside world and a port.

items.prompt: A folder named domain imports a database client. Is it hexagonal?
choices: Yes, because of its folder name
Yes, because the file count is right
No
items.explanation: The label means nothing without the enforced direction.

items.prompt: A lint rule fails the build when any file under domain/ imports from adapters/. What is that rule enforcing?
choices: The deployment boundary that makes the code microservices
The delivery guarantee that makes the code event-driven
The dependency direction that makes the code hexagonal
The layer order that makes the code a plainly layered one
items.explanation: It fixes the inward arrow, which is the structural rule behind hexagonal.
items.reference:
Same box count, different arrows
layered: lower layers can leak back up; nothing enforces it
hexagonal: adapters import the domain, never reverse
test: does the domain import a framework or adapter?
folder names prove nothing
Why: the difference is the enforced direction of imports.
items.learnMore:
Import direction

Both styles keep the code in one app, so their folder trees can look alike. A hexagonal codebase refuses imports that point from the domain out to infrastructure; a layered one usually does not.

Common mistake

Calling a codebase hexagonal because a folder is named domain. If that folder imports a database client, the arrow points the wrong way.
items.reflection: Where in a system or organization you know does something core depend on something peripheral when it should be the other way around? What would reversing that dependency look like?

items.prompt: Two codebases have identical folder trees. In one, domain files import a web framework. Which statement is true?
choices: Only the other one satisfies the hexagonal dependency rule
Both are hexagonal because their folders are identical
Neither can be layered because they have a domain folder
Both are microservices since they were split into folders
items.explanation: Structure is judged by import direction, not by how the folders look.

items.prompt: What does a sender do in an event-driven flow?
choices: Waits for the receiver to finish the work
Calls the receiver by name twice for safety
Publishes an event and returns right away
items.explanation: The sender announces what happened and moves on.

items.prompt: If the loyalty handler is down, what happens to the pricing service?
choices: It keeps working normally
It stops accepting new orders
It crashes and restarts repeatedly
items.explanation: The receiver's outage does not block a sender that only publishes.

items.prompt: What is the price of event-driven's loose coupling?
choices: The loss of all automated testing
Harder tracing of what happened
A required single large database
items.explanation: The trail is spread across logs instead of one call stack.

items.prompt: Does the sender learn whether the receiver succeeded?
choices: Not directly
Always, through the return value
Yes, within the same function call
items.explanation: That is the point: it never waits for the outcome.

items.prompt: What is 'eventual consistency'?
choices: Data is permanently lost after a short delay
Data is always identical in every location
Data is correct a little later, not instantly everywhere
items.explanation: Parts catch up with each other after some delay.

items.prompt: How does debugging change in event-driven systems?
choices: You read one call stack from top to bottom
You no longer need any logs of any kind
You read an event log and rebuild the timeline
items.explanation: Causes and effects are separated in time and place.

items.prompt: What does the sender no longer depend on?
choices: The receiver's uptime
Its own business logic
The event's shape
items.explanation: That independence is what the style buys.

items.prompt: A message left in an inbox for another team is like which style?
choices: Layered
Event-driven
Hexagonal
items.explanation: The sender leaves a note and the other team handles it later.

items.prompt: Pricing publishes OrderPriced and returns. Ten minutes later, a customer asks why no points arrived. What is the hardest part of answering?
choices: The pricing service returned the wrong total to the customer's screen
The customer's order was never actually saved
The event bus has no way to deliver messages
The cause lives in separate logs, not one call stack
items.explanation: Cause and effect are decoupled in time, so the answer needs correlating several logs.
items.reference:
Loose in time, not free
sender publishes and returns immediately
receiver acts later, maybe after retries
sender never learns the result
debugging means reading an event log
Why: the sender's correctness no longer depends on the receiver's uptime, but the trail is spread across logs.
items.learnMore:
What loose coupling moves

A direct call ties the sender to the receiver's speed and uptime. Publishing an event cuts that tie, and the knowledge of what happened moves into a log you must read and correlate.

Common mistake

Believing events remove coupling altogether. The event's shape is still shared, and timing now becomes a concern of its own.
items.reflection: Think of leaving a message instead of waiting on hold. What did you gain, and what did you stop being able to know right away? Where else in your life do you make that trade?

items.prompt: Which requirement is a good fit for publishing an event instead of calling directly?
choices: The receiver's answer decides the price of the order
Analytics should update without ever delaying checkout
The caller must show the receiver's result on screen right now
Two steps must succeed or fail together instantly
items.explanation: Only the first tolerates delay; the others need the receiver's answer immediately.

hexagonal: same wait behind a port (violates)

items.prompt: What does at-least-once delivery mean?
choices: An event arrives exactly once, always, with no repeats ever
An event arrives one or more times, never lost
An event may be silently lost sometimes
items.explanation: The bus prefers a duplicate over a lost event.

items.prompt: What is idempotency?
choices: Receiving the same event twice still performs the effect once
Sending every event to every single consumer registered on the bus
Deleting events after the first delivery
items.explanation: A repeat is harmless.

items.prompt: Who handles duplicates safely?
choices: The customer
The pricing producer
The consumer
items.explanation: The consumer is the one performing the side effect.

items.prompt: What does the handler remember to dedupe?
choices: The color of the event bus
The length of the order total in digits
An identifier such as the orderId
items.explanation: A stable id lets it recognize a repeat.

items.prompt: A duplicate OrderPriced arrives with no dedupe. What happens to points?
choices: They are awarded twice
They are awarded zero times
They are cancelled automatically
items.explanation: The handler runs the effect again.

items.prompt: An order total of 40 at one point per unit is delivered twice with no dedupe. Total points?
items.explanation: 40 + 40 = 80 under that assumption.

items.prompt: What does the event need to carry so the consumer can dedupe?
choices: A full copy of the customer database
The producer's source code
An identifier such as the order id
items.explanation: Without an id the consumer cannot tell a repeat.

items.prompt: What is the customer-visible effect of eventual consistency here?
choices: The order may complete before the points appear
Points appear before the order is placed
The order is cancelled until points arrive
items.explanation: Correct soon, rather than correct immediately.

items.prompt: The bus delivers OrderPriced #7 twice and the customer gets double points. Where is the defect?
choices: In the producer, which ought to publish each event only once
In the customer, who placed the same order twice
In the consumer, which does not recognize a repeat
In the discount math applied before publishing
items.explanation: At-least-once delivery is expected; handling it safely is the consumer's job.
items.reference:
At-least-once means duplicates happen
delivery 1: award 40 (assumed 40-point order)
delivery 2 (duplicate): without a check, award 40 again = 80
with a remembered orderId: skip the duplicate
event must carry an id the consumer can dedupe on
Why: prefer a duplicate to a lost event, then make a duplicate harmless.
items.learnMore:
Idempotent consumers

At-least-once delivery trades loss for repetition. The consumer cancels the downside by recognizing an event it has already handled, usually by an identifier carried in the event.

Common mistake

Putting the fix on the producer. Publishing twice is not the problem; handling twice is.
items.reflection: Where do you receive the same instruction twice in everyday life (a repeated form, a doubled text)? What do you do so that the second one causes no harm?

items.prompt: What is a distributed monolith?

A single app with many folders
A database stored on several disks
items.explanation: It has service costs without service independence.

items.prompt: Which symptom suggests a distributed monolith?
choices: A and B release on different days without trouble
Every change to A needs a same-day change to B
A has its own clear narrow interface
items.explanation: Lockstep releases mean the seam is not real.

items.prompt: What does a distributed monolith add over a plain monolith?

Network calls and extra pipelines

items.prompt: Does it deliver independent deployment?

Yes
Only on weekdays
items.explanation: The halves still move as one.

items.prompt: What is a good sign that a seam is real?

items.prompt: What does 'A cannot answer without calling B' suggest?

items.explanation: Without the rule enforced, imports leak and it becomes layered.

items.prompt: Services A and B were split last quarter. Every release needs both, scheduled together. How should this be described?

An event-driven system with a very slow message bus
A distributed monolith, with the cost but not the benefit of services
A hexagonal system whose ports were drawn too wide
